10.20377_jfr-1377#E4.says: Authors report men who do much less than fair share show no lower satisfaction, while the few women in that group show a strong negative association, so the pattern is gender dependent and rests on low cell counts.
10.20377_jfr-1377#E4.quote: Given low cell populations – especially for women who report doing much less than fair –, this pattern should, however, be interpreted with caution.

10.20377_jfr-1377#E5.says: The fairness item mixes housework and paid work and does not fix a standard of fair share, so "over-benefited" here is self-perceived under-contribution across both domains, not an allocation judged equitable or not by an external standard.
10.20377_jfr-1377#E5.quote: Looking at both housework and paid work: Overall, how fair is the division of labor between you and your partner?

10.20377_jfr-1377#E6.says: This study measures perceived fairness with one self-report item (five response options, housework and paid work combined); it is one instance of the single-item approach and is not evidence about how studies in general measure it.
10.20377_jfr-1377#E6.quote: Respondents could choose one of five response options: “I do much more than my fair share,” “I do a bit more than my fair share,” “I do roughly my fair share,” “I do a bit less than my fair share,” and “I do much more than my fair share;”

10.20377_jfr-1377#E7.says: Both the chore-split index (.365***, full sample) and the fairness categories (for example much more -1.381***) are entered in one model; the coefficients are unstandardised and on different scales, so the paper does not compare their strengths directly.

10.20377_jfr-1377#E8.says: Among men the index of household tasks coefficient is small and not significant (.129, SE .097) while fairness categories are significant, whereas for women it is .523*** (SE .094), so the relative role of the chore split differs by gender.

10.20377_jfr-1377#E9.says: The actual split of chores is operationalised as a mean index of seven self-reported household tasks and used only as a control variable alongside the fairness items.
10.20377_jfr-1377#E9.quote: We additionally control for an index capturing the within-couple distribution of seven household tasks.

10.20377_jfr-1377#E10.says: The authors rely on between-person differences and state that testing whether satisfaction responds to changes in the division requires longitudinal data; no mediation analysis of the split-satisfaction association through fairness is reported.
10.20377_jfr-1377#E10.quote: Moreover, it is important to note that we are relying on between-person differences to study the fairness-satisfaction relationship.

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E1.says: Authors conclude that women whose mothers did most housework are more likely to be in a class where she calls the division unfair, whatever the actual split (traditional or semi-equitable); this is a class-membership association, not a model of fairness conditional on the split.
10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E1.quote:
We find that
women who grew up in traditional-housework homes are more likely to occupy a
cluster where she views the housework as unfair, regardless of the actual division
(traditional and semi-equitable).

tier_b.caveat: Outcome is cluster membership versus equal/fair couples; split differs between clusters, so fairness is not modelled net of the split.

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E2.says: Table 3 row for the comparative referent "her mother traditional": coefficient 1.189 (p<0.001) for class 2, 0.713 (p<0.10) for class 3 and 0.481 (p<0.05) for class 5, relative to class 4; no standard errors given.

tier_b.caveat: Different outcome: cluster membership versus equal/fair class; classes 2-3 differ in split too; only class 5 approximates equal split; class 3 p<0.10.

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E3.says: The predictors are tested against modal class membership (classes built from the share and fairness indicators), not against fairness with the actual split held constant.
10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E3.quote:
Class membership is determined by the class that the couple has the highest probability
of belonging to, based on the couple’s sharing behavior, the woman’s perception of
fairness, and the partners’ agreement on the fairness. We then examine how variables
such as housework socialization, gender ideology, work status, and educational
achievement predict such class membership, using multinomial logistic regressions.

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E4.says: Table 3 row for "she more egalitarian" (a justification): 0.663 (p<0.05) for class 3 (both say unfair to her), 0.449 (p<0.10) for class 2, relative to class 4.

tier_b.caveat: Class 3 differs from reference in split too; at semi-equal split (class 5) coefficient is 0.165, non-significant; relative ideology, not an accepted justification.

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E5.says: Authors report that women's reduced employment does not act as a justification: women in classes 2 and 3 call the inequality unfair, contrary to earlier research; so justification effects are mixed.
10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E5.quote:
However, counter
to previous research, women’s reduced labor force participation does not ‘justify’ this
housework inequality, as women in these couples view their housework inequality as
unfair (groups 2 and 3).

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E6.says: For class 1 (semi-traditional, she fair, he unfair) no distributive-justice predictor (referents or justifications) is significant; only a child in the home is.
10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E6.quote:
However, we
find no support for the distributive justice perspective explaining this group
membership. Rather, we find that respondents in this category are more likely to have a
child in the home than equal sharing/fair couples (our comparison group).

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E7.says: Couples with semi-equal splits fall into class 4 (both fair) or class 5 (she unfair, he fair), so fairness differs at similar splits; no variance-explained figure is given, so the claim of a small explained share is untested.
10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E7.quote:
Group 5 includes couples with semi-equal housework allocations, allowing us to
compare couples where women view this as unfair but men view it as fair (group 5) to
those where both partners view equal housework as fair (group 4).

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E8.says: This study measures perceived fairness of the housework division with a single survey question (one five-option self-report item per partner); it is one study, so it shows the practice, not its prevalence.
10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E8.quote:
The perception of fairness regarding the sharing of housework is measured by the
question “Which of the following statements do you think applies to your household?

10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E9.says: The single fairness item is a five-point scale of over- to under-doing one's fair share, recoded to run from the woman doing much more than her fair share to the man doing much more.
10.4054_demres.2017.36.16#E9.quote:
We recoded the variable on a five-point scale to reflect
gendered fairness ranging from a) the woman does much more than her fair share, to e)
the man does much more than his fair share.

10.5153_sro.3871#E1.says: Most women (62.8%) and men (57.4%) call their share fair even though women do about two thirds and men one third of chores, so the split and perceived fairness are loosely coupled; no variance explained is reported, so the claim is not tested directly.
10.5153_sro.3871#E1.quote: most women (62.8%) and men (57.4%) reported that their share of housework is fair, although the former do on average two thirds of the chores and the latter about one third

tier_b.caveat: Shows fairness levels against mean shares, not covariation; 'loosely coupled' goes beyond the passage, and no variance explained is reported.

10.5153_sro.3871#E2.says: Women's average share (two thirds) and men's (one third) sum to about one, which gives no sign of over-claiming on average, but the figures are rounded, unpaired by couple and "results not shown", so they do not test the sum within couples.
10.5153_sro.3871#E2.quote: most women (62.8%) and men (57.4%) reported that their share of housework is fair, although the former do on average two thirds of the chores and the latter about one third

10.5153_sro.3871#E3.says: The survey models control for the respondent's own percentage of housework and childcare, working hours and paid help, so comparison effects are estimated net of a measure of the actual split.
10.5153_sro.3871#E3.quote: we selected variables representing the division of responsibilities within the couple: respondent's and spouse's working hours, respondent's percentage of housework, respondent's percentage of childcare

tier_b.caveat: Passage describes the control variables only; it shows no referent effect itself.

10.5153_sro.3871#E4.says: The control for the actual split is a respondent-reported estimate built from frequency questions, so it is a noisy measure and leaves room for residual confounding of the referent effect.
10.5153_sro.3871#E4.quote: Respondent's percentage of housework and childcare was estimated using answers to several questions about the frequency of housework and care tasks.

10.5153_sro.3871#E5.says: The expected significant effects of favourable and unfavourable comparisons on fairness are generally found for men comparing themselves with men and for women comparing their husband with men, with controls for the split.
10.5153_sro.3871#E5.quote: the expected significant effect of both favorable and unfavorable comparisons on fairness perception is generally found when male respondents compare themselves with other same-sex referents and when female respondents do the same with their partner's behavior.

10.5153_sro.3871#E6.says: Referent effects are null for comparisons involving women (women's own comparisons with women, men's comparisons of their wife), so the claim holds only for some referents.
10.5153_sro.3871#E6.quote: No significant effect is found either when women compare themselves with their female counterparts (mothers, friends, the average Italian woman), or when men do the same with their partner's domestic contribution.

10.5153_sro.3871#E7.says: For husbands comparing themselves with a male friend, the predicted probability of "fair" falls from 0.56 (same time) to 0.40 (does less), a 0.16 drop.
10.5153_sro.3871#E7.quote: when a husband thinks he does the same amount of housework of his male friend, the probability of evaluating the housework division as fair is 0.56. If he thinks does less, the probability decreases to 0.40.

10.5153_sro.3871#E8.says: For wives comparing their husband with their father, the predicted probability of "fair" falls from 0.63 to 0.45 when the husband does less than the father.
10.5153_sro.3871#E8.quote: If in wife's opinion her father did the same amount of housework than her husband, the probability of evaluating the housework division as fair is 0.63; if her husband does less, the probability decreases to 0.45.

10.5153_sro.3871#E9.says: The authors themselves suspect that self-serving bias distorts the choice of referents in the survey, so the survey associations may overstate the referent effect.
10.5153_sro.3871#E9.quote: Although these results do show an effect of men's behavior as comparison referent, we may suspect that self-serving bias has a distorting effect on the choice of referents.

10.5153_sro.3871#E10.says: The randomised vignette outcome is a behavioural-change judgment about a fictitious husband, not a direct fairness judgment, so it only indirectly bears on fairness.
10.5153_sro.3871#E10.quote: This, of course, is not a direct judgment of fairness, but we assumed that such a behavioral change will, in the long run, be followed by a corresponding change in perceived fairness in order to avoid cognitive dissonance.

10.5153_sro.3871#E11.says: In the randomised vignette, friends who share housework equally raise the subjective probability that the husband does more by 6.9 percentage points; the effect is on a behavioural-intention outcome and is not conditional on the actual split.
10.5153_sro.3871#E11.quote: the probability that Riccardo will do more at home increases, as expected, if his friends share housework equally rather than if they do almost nothing (+6.9 percentage points).

tier_b.caveat: Outcome is a behavioural-change probability, not fairness; the vignette fixes the split (wife does almost all), so it is held constant, not ignored.

10.5153_sro.3871#E12.says: The authors conclude from the survey data that referential and normative comparisons and past family models play a significant role in fairness evaluation.
10.5153_sro.3871#E12.quote: The findings from survey data show that referential and normative comparisons, as well as past family models, do in fact play a significant role in housework fairness evaluation.

10.5153_sro.3871#E13.says: This study measures perceived fairness with a single self-report item on a 5-point scale (then dichotomised); it is one study and the paper does not survey how other studies measure fairness, so it is an instance rather than evidence of the "mainly" pattern.
10.5153_sro.3871#E13.quote: It was probed with the following question: 'Regarding the division of housework with your partner, do you personally think that what you do is… (1 - Much more than fair, 2 - A bit more than fair, 3 - Fair, 4 - A little less than fair or 5 - Much less than fair)?'

tier_b.caveat: One study's own measure; says nothing about what most studies use, so it cannot support 'mainly'.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E1.says: In this large panel study the perceived-fairness outcome is one self-report item on whether the respondent does their fair share, then collapsed to a binary.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E1.quote: Therefore, our outcome variable measures whether individuals perceive the domestic division of labor to be unfair to them

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E2.says: The authors state that they operationalise fairness with a single HILDA variable on doing more than, less than or one's fair share of housework.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E2.quote:
To operationalize the concept we use a variable in
the HILDA Survey capturing whether individuals perceive that they do more than, less than, or their fair share of work
around the house.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E1.says: Standardized path from segregation to fairness is -.36 (Moslem women, ns), -.38 and -.39 (Christian and Jewish women, p < .01); this implies a modest share of fairness variance (about 13 to 15%, my arithmetic) but the paper reports no variance explained.

tier_b.caveat: Variance explained not reported; the 13-15% is the reader's derivation from standardized paths; Moslem estimate non-significant.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E2.says: In the pooled models the split-to-fairness path is -.36 for women and only -.25 (not significant) for men, so the split accounts for a small part of fairness variance for women and none detectable for men.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E2.quote: FIGURE 1. STANDARDIZED COEFFICIENTS FOR A MODEL OF PERCEIVED FAIRNESS AS MEDIATOR BETWEEN SEGREGATED DIVISION OF LABOR AND MARITAL QUALITY--ESTIMATES FOR MEN AND WOMEN
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E2.read: Women: Segregation to Fairness -.36, Fairness to Marital Quality .45, Segregation to Marital Quality -.13 (dashed). Men: Segregation to Fairness -.25 (dashed, not significant), Fairness to Marital Quality .51, Segregation to Marital Quality -.04 (dashed).

tier_b.caveat: value read from the figure; only the caption is checkable

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E1.says: Reports, from Thompson (1991), the argument that a wife sees an unequal split as unfair only if she compares her husband with someone doing more; this is stated as an argument, not as a tested association net of the actual split, and carries no effect size.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E1.quote: She argues that women will perceive the division of household labor as unfair only if they want their husbands to perform more housework, if they compare their husband's housework time to someone who spends more time on housework, and if they do not see any justification for the unequal division of housework.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E1.says: In 25 interviewed couples, wives who discussed household setups with peers were more likely to call the split fair to both; no count, no adjustment for the actual split.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E1.quote: Overall, wives who were privy to the details of their friends' or siblings' household setups, or who talked with women in similar circumstances, were more likely to report that their division of labor was fair to both spouses.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E2.says: The author concludes from interviews that same-sex, same-status referents play an important role in fairness evaluations; qualitative, untested net of the split.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E2.quote: My interview data indicate that choice of same-sex and same-status comparison referents plays an important role in evaluations of fairness in the division of household labor.

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E1.says: Table 2 gives the association of perceived unfairness with marital happiness (-6.734 points for men, -3.342 for women, p < .001) but the actual split is not in the model, so the fairness coefficient is not compared with the split's.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E1.quote:
R does more than his or her fair share
–6.734*** (1.719)
–3.342***
(.418)

tier_b.caveat: Table column headers absent from passage; that the outcome is marital happiness and which column is men versus women is not checkable here.

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E2.says: Reports, from Perry-Jenkins and Folk (1994) and Wilkie et al. (1998), that perceived equity matters more to marital satisfaction than the proportion of housework; this study did not test the comparison itself.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E2.quote:
Other studies find that perceived equity in the
household division of labor is more important to marital satisfaction and
conflict than the proportion of housework completed by each spouse
(Perry-Jenkins & Folk, 1994; Wilkie, Ferree, & Ratcliff, 1998).

tier_b.caveat: Finding attributed to Perry-Jenkins & Folk (1994) and Wilkie et al. (1998); asserts the claim but this study did not test it.

10.1177_089124398012002005#E1.says: Both sexes report more weekly hours on four chores in the direct-question survey than in the diary survey (wives 31.8 vs 18.4, husbands 7.7 vs 4.2), which is overreport against a diary baseline in different samples, not a sum of partners' shares above the whole.
10.1177_089124398012002005#E1.quote: On average, wives estimate they perform about 31.8 hours a week but only record about 18.4 hours in the time diaries. Husbands self-report their housework at 7.7 hours per week but record only 4.2 hours in the diaries.

10.1177_2378023118765867#E1.says: The exposures are the divisions of seven individual tasks (five routine, two nonroutine) and the outcomes are relationship quality measures; perceived fairness is not an outcome.
10.1177_2378023118765867#E1.quote:
We examine the association of seven
individual household tasks with couples’ relationship quality.
Routine housework tasks include preparing and cooking
meals, washing dishes, cleaning around the house, shopping
for groceries, and doing laundry. Nonroutine tasks include
home maintenance or outdoor tasks and bill paying.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E3.says: Parenthood effects on women's perceived unfairness weaken only slightly when the actual split, time and resources are controlled, so the measured objective factors leave much of the change unaccounted for; no variance explained is reported.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E3.quote:
Strikingly, the effects of parenthood on perceived housework fairness
amongst women weaken only slightly when all the relevant objective factors are included in the model.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E4.says: The authors conclude that time availability and relative resources explain some but not all of the change in perceived fairness across transitions; this is a statement about change, not variance explained by the split.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E4.quote:
Having established that time availability and relative resources can explain some, but not all, changes in perceptions of
housework fairness across life course transitions

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E5.says: Within-person odds ratio on the respondent's share of couple housework hours is 5.98 for women and 7.13 for men (Table 3, Model 3); the split is a strong predictor, and no variance explained is reported.

tier_b.caveat: Row not in shown passage; women/men column order and Model 3 cannot be confirmed; an odds ratio is not variance explained.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E6.says: Comparison referents and other distributive-justice factors are not measured in HILDA; they are tested only as a residual, so C2 is not directly tested.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E6.quote:
As explained before, the subjective dispositions proposed by the distributive justice perspective are typically unmeasured
or unmeasurable in survey data and consequently impossible to model directly in a quantitative framework.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E7.says: The authors call for survey items that ask directly about comparison referents, confirming none were available; their inference about subjective mechanisms depends on having controlled every instrumental factor.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E7.quote:
However, we can only declare that subjective dispositions are in fact behind the relationships
between life course transitions and perceptions of housework fairness if we assume that our model contains all possible
instrumental factors inﬂuencing perceptions of housework fairness.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E8.says: Measures of the subjective factors, including who one compares to and impediments to equal sharing, are described as not routinely available in quantitative studies; justifications accepted for an unequal split are not measured here.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E8.quote: Such data are not routinely available in quantitative empirical studies.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E9.says: The authors state that psychological mechanisms can be tested only by an indirect residual approach, so no direct test of accepted justifications is made.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E9.quote:
As mentioned above, we can only test the psychological mechanisms suggested by the distributive justice perspective
using an indirect or residual approach.

10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E10.says: The actual division is entered as total couple weekly housework hours and the respondent's share of hours; which chores are done is not measured, so C7 is untested.
10.1016_j.ssresearch.2014.12.010#E10.quote:
factors capturing the actual household division of labor (total couple weekly housework hours and respondent’s share of the housework
hours)

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E1.says: The reviewer concludes, as his main conclusion across reviewed studies, that the actual division of household labor is not the main determinant of perceived justice; no figure is given for the share of variance.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E1.quote: The main conclusion to be drawn is that the actual division of household labor is by no means the main determinant of perceptions of justice.

tier_b.caveat: Says the split is not the main determinant; this sentence alone does not state that its share of variance is small.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E2.says: Reports across studies that the variance in fairness ratings explained by quantitative workload measures is relatively small (no figure given); this is about quantitative workload measures, a proxy for the actual split.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E2.quote: the amount of variation in the fairness ratings which can be explained by measures of quantitative… aspects of the division of workload is relatively small.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E3.says: Reports, from Hawkins et al. (1995) and other studies, that a cognition-rich model explained 66% of wives' fairness variance while most other studies explained no more than 20% (all predictors, not the split alone), so the share due to the split alone is not given.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E3.quote: who were able to account for 66% of the variance in wives' perception of fairness about household labor, while most other studies explained no more than 20% of the variation in the justice ratings.

tier_b.caveat: Whole models in most studies explain at most 20%, which bounds the split's share as small; split-specific share not given.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E4.says: Reports, from Mederer (1993), a final model with three household-labor measures plus controls explaining more than 50% of fairness variance, which the reviewer discounts as an exception because her fairness measure overlapped the predictors.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E4.quote: Her final model, which included three measures of household labor besides control variables, explained more than 50% of the variance of the fairness ratings.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E5.says: Reports, from Hawkins et al. (1995), a significant correlation of between-gender comparison with lower perceived fairness among wives; zero-order association, no statement that the actual split was controlled.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E5.quote: Wives regarded the division of labor less fair the more they compared their husbands' contributions to housework with their own contributions and not with the contributions of other men.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E6.says: Reports, from Grote and Clark (1998b, unpublished), that more frequent between-gender comparison went with lower fairness for both sexes, and that within-gender comparison also went with lower fairness, contrary to Major's expectation; covariate set not stated.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E6.quote: the frequency of making between-gender comparisons with the spouse was negatively related to perceived fairness for both women and men.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E7.says: The reviewer notes that the causal direction between comparison and perceived injustice is undetermined (injustice may prompt comparison), so prediction of fairness by referents cannot be read causally.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E7.quote: There is no evidence available that allows one to decide between the two possibilities.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E8.says: Reports, from Hawkins et al. (1995), the 66% of variance explained for wives' fairness by a model of cognitions (which include comparison referents), but this is the whole model, not referents net of the actual split.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E8.quote: who were able to account for 66% of the variance in wives' perception of fairness about household labor

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E9.says: Reports, from Hawkins et al. (1995), that wives perceived more fairness when the division was worked out together (a procedural justification); no effect size or adjustment for the actual split is given.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E9.quote: They found that women perceived more fairness when they reported that the division of household labor had been worked out together.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E10.says: Reports, from Freudenthaler and Mikula (1998), that perceived lack of justification contributed only indirectly, through blaming the partner, to women's sense of injustice, not as a direct predictor.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E10.quote: perceived lack of justification and attributions of responsibility to the partner for not doing more housework contributed indirectly to the experience of injustice through their impact on the blaming of the partner.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E11.says: Reports, from Hawkins et al. (1995), 66% of wives' fairness variance explained by a model of cognitions (justifications among them); whole-model figure, not justifications net of the actual split.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E11.quote: who were able to account for 66% of the variance in wives' perception of fairness about household labor

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E12.says: Reports, from Blair (1993, 1998), Greenstein (1996) and Ward (1993), that studies including both measures typically found perceived justice a more important indicator of marital quality than the division of housework; no coefficients given.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E12.quote: studies that considered the division of household labor in addition to the perception of justice typically found that the perception of justice was a more important indicator of marital quality than was the division of housework itself

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E13.says: Reports, from Perry-Jenkins and Folk (1994), an exception in which, for working-class wives, the division of feminine tasks rather than perceived equity was the more consistent indicator of marital conflict.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E13.quote: for working-class wives, the more consistent indicator of frequency of marital conflict was not equity but the division of (feminine) household tasks.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E14.says: Reports that the fairness association with satisfaction and marital quality is stronger for women than men across several studies, so the claim holds unevenly by partner.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E14.quote: much of the available evidence suggests that the associations between perceived fairness and measures of satisfaction, marital quality, and psychological well-being are stronger with women than with men

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E15.says: The reviewer states that whether perceived injustice mediates between the division of labor and marital quality has had little systematic study.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E15.quote: psychological well-being has received little systematic attention thus far.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E16.says: Reports, from Robinson and Spitze (1992), that for women only the housework-share association with well-being vanished after controlling for perceived fairness; the outcome is well-being, not relationship satisfaction.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E16.quote: who found for women, but not for men, that the association between women's housework share and well-being disappeared after controlling for perceived fairness

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E17.says: Reports, from Reichle's work with new parents, that injustice perceptions affect emotional responses to restrictions which in turn mediate marital satisfaction; the exposure is restrictions after a birth, not the chore split.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E17.quote: perceptions of injustice, and attributions of responsibility for the experienced restrictions, affect the emotional responses to these restrictions, which in turn mediate marital satisfaction.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E18.says: The reviewer says only that perceived injustice may distort respondents' estimates of own and partner contributions; over-claiming by both partners (shares summing above 100%) is not reported or tested.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E18.quote: Perceptions of injustice may well distort the estimation of own and partner's contributions to the housework.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E19.says: Reports, from several studies, that contributions to female-type tasks predict perceived justice better than male-type, neutral or global task measures; a comparison of correlations, not a test beyond time spent.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E19.quote:
Contributions to female-type tasks (e.g., cooking, cleaning, doing laun-
dry) are better predictors of perceived justice than contributions to male-
type tasks (outdoor tasks, car maintenance)

tier_b.caveat: Different comparator: compares predictive power of task types, not task type net of time spent.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E20.says: The reviewer infers from the pattern of correlations (men's share of female-type tasks highest) that task meaning matters more than the amount of time and effort; an inference from correlations, not a covariate-adjusted test.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E20.quote: the nature of the measures of family labor which showed the highest correlations with the ratings of fairness (e.g., men's contributions to female-type household tasks) suggests that the symbolic meaning of men's and women's contributions to family work is much more relevant than the mere amount of time and effort.

tier_b.caveat: Reviewer's interpretation of zero-order correlations ('suggests'); no analysis of task type adjusted for time spent.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E21.says: The reviewer says the NSFH one-item fairness measure underlies most recent studies and that one-item measures of questionable reliability are common to many studies; the studies are not counted.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E21.quote:
One problem which studies using NSHF data share with many other
studies is the use of one-item measures of questionable reliability.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E22.says: Identifies the single NSFH fairness item as the basis of the most common database of recent studies of the division of family work, naming about ten studies using it.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E22.quote: the measure of fairness used in the National Survey of Families and Households (NSFH; Sweet et al., 1988), which provides the most common database of recent studies about the division of family work

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E23.says: Notes that some studies used composite scores mixing fairness and satisfaction, so not all studies used a single fairness item; no tally of measure types is given.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E23.quote: Further studies calculated composite scores of fairness and satisfaction ratings (e.g., Mederer, 1993)

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E24.says: Reports the equity-theory prediction (Walster et al., 1978) that under-benefit is more distressing than over-benefit, which if anything predicts a smaller effect of over-benefit; no study of over-benefit and relationship satisfaction is reported.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E24.quote: the equity theoretical prediction that underbenefiting inequity will be more easily recognized and lead to more distress than overbenefiting inequity

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E25.says: Reports, from two student-household studies (Mikula et al. 1997a), that a smaller own share and higher perceived fairness each predicted more satisfaction with the division of housework; the outcome is satisfaction with the division, not with the relationship.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E25.quote:
were more satisfied with the division of housework the more fair they re-
garded the division and the smaller the relative size of their own share to
the housework was.

10.1023_a-1023282615718#E26.says: The reviewer reasons that unfair divisions generally benefit men and disadvantage women, who are therefore more attuned to fairness; this implies weaker fairness-satisfaction links for the over-benefited, as an interpretation and not a tested result.
10.1023_a-1023282615718#E26.quote:
unfair divisions of housework generally benefit men but place
women at a disadvantage, which may lead the latter to be more attuned
to perceived fairness

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E3.says: For men the degree of labor segregation did not significantly affect fairness at all.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E3.quote:
Although sense of fairness is positively related to marital quality, it
is not affected by the degree of household labor segregation.

tier_b.caveat: Men only; a non-significant path is undetected, not shown to be small.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E4.says: The authors attribute Christian Arab women's lower fairness to a gap between the actual division and expectations shaped by egalitarian referents, but referents were not measured; this is interpretation, with group as the only proxy.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E4.quote:
It appears that for these women a gap ex-
ists between the actual division of labor, which is
shaped by traditional family patterns, and their ex-
pectations, which are influenced by egalitarian ref-
erents.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E5.says: For Moslem women the authors again invoke referents (ideologically similar others) to explain why a very segregated split is not seen as unfair; offered as one of several untested explanations.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E5.quote:
Second, these women base their
expectations on referents that are ideologically
similar to themselves and thus justify the lesser
participation of their husbands in the domestic
sphere

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E6.says: The idea that accepted justifications keep an unequal split from feeling unfair appears only as a post hoc explanation for Moslem women, among three possibilities; no justification measure or adjusted estimate exists in the study.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E6.quote:
Although
the division of labor in their families is the most
traditionally segregated along gender lines, it is
not perceived as unfair but rather as equitable.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E7.says: Women's standardized fairness-to-marital-quality path is .38 (Moslem, ns), .76 (Christian, p < .01) and .03 (Jewish, ns), so fairness outranks the split only in some groups.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E8.says: Women's standardized direct segregation-to-marital-quality path is -.04, -.10 and -.46 (only the Jewish estimate is significant), the reverse of the fairness row: for Jewish women the split matters more than fairness.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E9.says: In the pooled mediated models fairness is the stronger correlate of marital quality: .45 vs -.13 (ns) for women and .51 vs -.04 (ns) for men; fairness and the split are in the same model.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E11.says: For women pooled across groups, the direct path becomes non-significant once fairness is added, which the authors read as full mediation (no indirect-effect interval reported).

the
direct effect of segregation on marital quality is no longer significant, indicating that the link between these variables is mediated by sense of

tier_b.caveat: Women subgroup only; mediation inferred from loss of significance, no formal indirect-effect test.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E12.says: For men fairness did not mediate: the split did not move fairness, although fairness predicted marital quality.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E12.quote:
For men, however, sense of fairness does not
function as a mediator variable.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E13.says: By group, mediation held only for Christian Arab women; Moslem women showed no segregation effects and Jewish women a direct split effect with fairness unrelated to marital quality.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E13.quote:
For the Jewish women, in
contrast, segregation is negatively related to both

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E14.says: Fairness here is a single self-report item modelled from the NSFH-I item, recoded to three categories.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E14.quote:
Sense of fairness was measured
by a single item similar to that used in the first
wave of the National Survey of Families and
Households (NSFH-I).

tier_b.caveat: One study's own measure; prevalence across studies is not shown by this passage.

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E15.says: The authors state that the single item is the most commonly used measure of fairness of the division of household labor in earlier studies including NSFH-I, while noting it may create interpretive difficulties (cites Smith, Gager & Morgan 1998); secondary statement about the literature.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E15.quote:
Although
this item has been the most commonly used mea-
sure in previous studies of fairness in the division
of household labor, including the NSFH-I project,
it may create some difficulties in interpretation

10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E16.says: Over-benefited respondents (self-perceived "unfair to my spouse") were only 2.1% of women and 3.9% of men, and a sensitivity analysis (no estimates given) found their marital quality similar to those saying the division was fair; this tends against C9 but is untested, tiny and based on perceived rather than allocated over-benefit.
10.1111_j.1741-3737.2002.00027.x#E16.quote: only 2.1% of women and 3.9% of men perceived the division of labor to be…unfair or very unfair to their spouses. In a sensitivity analysis, these respondents were found to be similar in terms of their division of household…and marital quality to those who perceived the division of labor to be fair.

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E2.says: Reports, from Thompson (1991) and Major (1994), that comparing oneself with other women rather than with the husband may lead a woman to see an unequal split as fair; direction is given but no adjusted estimate.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E2.quote: Moreover, if women compare their housework time to other women's, rather than to their husband's time, they may view an unequal division of household labor as fair (Major 1994, Thompson 1991).

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E3.says: Reports, from Thompson (1991), that women who see acceptable reasons for an unequal split will not view it as unfair, with acceptable reasons possibly varying by gender; a theoretical statement with no test or estimate given in the review.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E3.quote: Finally, if women see acceptable reasons for the unequal division of household labor, they will not view it as unfair (Thompson 1991), although the justifications viewed as acceptable may vary by gender (LaRossa & LaRossa 1981, McKee 1982).

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E4.says: The review calls the findings on the link between the actual division and perceived fairness inconsistent across studies; it gives no variance explained, so the size of the link is untested here.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E4.quote: In research evaluating the association between the division of household labor and perceptions of fairness, findings are inconsistent.

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E5.says: The reviewers suggest that ideological factors (Thompson 1991) may partly account for the inconsistent division-fairness findings, which hints that the split alone is not enough but is not quantified.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E5.quote: Thompson's (1991) argument that ideological factors affect perceptions of fairness may partially account for the inconsistent findings with respect to the relationship between the division of household labor and perceptions of fairness.

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E6.says: Reports, from several studies, that wives' marital satisfaction is higher when they feel the husband does a fair share, but few studies find a consistent relation between the actual division and satisfaction; this is in the direction of C4 for women but is a vote-count summary with no effect sizes and no head-to-head comparison.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E6.quote: Generally, these studies have found that women's marital satisfaction is higher when they feel their husbands do their "fair share" of housework, but few find any consistent relationship between the division of household labor and marital satisfaction

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E7.says: Reports, from Robinson & Spitze (1992), that men's marital happiness is affected by their housework time but not by their perceptions of fairness, effects modest; for men this runs against the claim that fairness is the stronger correlate.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E7.quote: Some research suggests that men's marital happiness is affected by their housework time, but not by their perceptions of fairness (perhaps because so few men view the division of household labor as unfair to themselves), but the effects are modest (Robinson & Spitze 1992).

tier_b.caveat: Men only, one study; fairness null not quantified, and the review attributes it to little variation in men's fairness perceptions.

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E8.says: Reports, from Pina & Bengston (1993), that the effect of the division on several satisfaction measures is mediated by perceived fairness, for wives; the review gives no design, size or test of mediation and the cited study is secondary reporting here.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E8.quote: Pina & Bengston (1993) find that the effect of the division of household labor on various measures of marital satisfaction is mediated by perceptions of how fairly housework is divided, with not all women viewing an unequal division of household labor as unfair.

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E9.says: Reports, from Marini & Shelton (1993), that respondents typically overestimate their own housework time and underestimate others'; this is in the direction of over-claiming, but it speaks of time estimates not shares and does not report that the two partners' shares sum to more than the whole.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E9.quote: Respondents typically overestimate their own housework time and underestimate the time spent by other household members (Marini & Shelton 1993)

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E10.says: Reports, from Blair & Johnson (1992), that men's time on female-typed tasks is the strongest predictor of wives' perceived fairness; this points to task type mattering but the passage does not say whether it adds to total time, and the review adds that Lennon & Rosenfield (1994) find the proportional share of female-typed tasks instead.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E10.quote: Blair & Johnson (1992) report that men's time spent on female-typed household tasks is the strongest predictor of women's perceptions of fairness

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E11.says: Reports, from John et al (1995), that both women and men are less likely to see the split as unfair as the man's proportional share of female-typed tasks rises; task type is the exposure but no comparison with total time or adjusted estimate is given.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E11.quote: John et al (1995) report that both women and men are less likely to view the division of household labor as unfair as the men's proportional share of female-typed tasks increases.

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E12.says: Reports, from Yogev & Brett (1985), that men's marital satisfaction is highest when they do what they consider their fair share, implying lower satisfaction when under-contributing (over-benefited); no figures and no direct over-benefited versus equitable contrast.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E12.quote: Yogev & Brett (1985) report that men's marital satisfaction is highest for men when they do what they consider to be their "fair share."

tier_b.caveat: Men only; fair share is self-defined, and lower satisfaction when over-benefited is inferred from 'highest at fair share', not a tested contrast.

10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E13.says: Reports, from Robinson & Spitze (1992), that men are happier in marriage when they do less housework, with proportional share not significant; for men, doing less (a likely over-benefited position) goes with higher, not lower, happiness.
10.1146_annurev.soc.22.1.299#E13.quote: Robinson & Spitze (1992) find that men report higher marital happiness when they spend less time on housework, but that men's proportional share of housework is not significant

tier_b.caveat: Different exposure: absolute hours, not over-benefit; the closer measure, proportional share, was non-significant, not a precise null.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E3.says: For parental referents, the author finds they do not sufficiently explain outcomes and perceptions, so not all referents predict fairness.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E3.quote: Thus, parental comparison referents and socialization cannot sufficiently explain adult choices and outcomes (see also Goldscheider & Waite, 1991).

tier_b.caveat: Passage says parental models influence fairness but do not determine it; it does not show parental referents fail to predict fairness.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E4.says: The most overburdened wives could not justify their outcomes and called the split unfair, so the effect of justifications depends on the actual split (qualitative, no estimate).
10.1177_019251398019005007#E4.quote: For instance, among the wives I interviewed, those who were the most overburdened by housework were unable to justify their outcomes, describing their division of labor as unfair to them.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E5.says: The author reports that justifications played a large part in spouses' formulations of a fair division, from interviews only.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E5.quote: Like Hochschild (1989), I found that justifications played a large part in spouses' formulations of what constitutes a fair division of labor.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E6.says: Wives with lower marital quality were more likely to see the split as unfair; an interview association with no comparison to the actual split, and no effect size.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E6.quote: Wives who reported lower marital quality were more likely to think that the division of family work was imbalanced or unfair.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E7.says: Reports, from refs including Blair 1994, Greenstein 1996, Suitor 1991, that fairness and marital happiness are strongly positively linked in NSFH and other data; says nothing of the split's association.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E7.quote: This strong positive link between perceptions of fairness and marital happiness has also been documented by researchers using the NSFH and other data sets

10.1177_019251398019005007#E8.says: Reports, from Blair & Johnson 1992 and Sanchez 1994, that objective and other survey variables have little explanatory power for fairness; secondary, with no R-squared given.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E8.quote: Most of the variables, although they bear some relationship to fairness, have little explanatory power (Blair & Johnson, 1992; Sanchez, 1994).

tier_b.caveat: Different quantity: survey variables in general have little explanatory power, not the actual split specifically; secondary summary with no variance estimate.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E9.says: Reports, from Thompson (1991), little success predicting fairness from time in housework and paid work or the specific tasks performed; does not test tasks beyond time.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E9.quote: scholars have had little success predicting spouses' sense of fairness about household labor using variables available in most national survey data sets such as time spent in housework and paid work or the specific tasks performed (Thompson, 1991)

10.1177_019251398019005007#E10.says: This study measured fairness by a single NSFH item on household chores, in a short questionnaire alongside the interviews.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E10.quote: included a question on fairness from the NSFH: "How do you feel about the fairness in your relationship in the following area: household chores?"

tier_b.caveat: One study, and its main fairness evidence came from qualitative interviews; the single NSFH item was a supplementary questionnaire measure.

10.1177_019251398019005007#E11.says: States that most prior work on fairness used NSFH survey data (the single-item fairness measure) as the outcome in regressions; the paper does not name the item here.
10.1177_019251398019005007#E11.quote: Most prior work on fairness in the division of household labor has been based on survey data from the NSFH and has involved regressing fairness on a series of predictors

tier_b.caveat: Passage says prior work used NSFH survey data; it does not say the fairness measure is a single item (elsewhere called the 'NSFH fairness scale').

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E3.says: The data held only a categorical self-report of the proportion done (all, most, half, less than half, none) and no hours measure, and the actual split was used only in a cross-tabulation, not in the models.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E3.quote:
Ideally, we would have liked to examine the actual number of hours of housework that
men and women report completing, but our data only provide us with a measure of whether
or not respondents feel they complete all, most, half, less than half, or none.

tier_b.caveat: Passage confirms only a categorical proportion measure; that the split was excluded from the models is not shown here.

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E4.says: The only mediation tested is perceived fairness to divorce through marital happiness (women: effect slightly reduced, still significant); the split-to-satisfaction path through fairness is not tested.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E4.quote:
We find that, among women, the effect of unfair perceptions of house-
work completion on divorce does slightly decrease, but the effect is still
statistically significant.

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E5.says: Perceived fairness is measured with one self-report item ("Do you think this is fair, or do you think you do more than your share?") with three response categories.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E5.quote:
“Do you think this is fair, or do you think you do more than your share?”
Response categories include “fair,” “I do more than my own share,”, and
“other.”

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E6.says: The study cannot test over-benefit: the only unfair group is those doing more than their share, and the other-does-more response is folded into an "other" category the authors say cannot be interpreted.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E6.quote:
However, we make no attempt to interpret coefficients for this variable be-
cause it is not possible to determine what a response of “other” means.

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E7.says: Descriptively (Table 4, no controls), 62.5% of women who judge the split fair report doing all or most of the housework, so the actual proportion does not fix perceived fairness; no variance-explained figure for the split is given.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E7.quote:
Among dual-earners who perceive
that the distribution of household labor is fair, 62.5% of women report do-
ing all or most of the housework.

10.1177_0192513x02238520#E8.says: 81.5% of men who call the split unfair report doing only half or less, so the same perceived unfairness goes with very different actual splits for men and women.
10.1177_0192513x02238520#E8.quote:
However, almost all of the men (81.5%) who
define the household distribution of labor as unfair report completing only
half or less than half of the housework.

The perception of fairness in the division of household labor, the dependent
variable, was tapped with a single item from the NSFH that asked "How do

tier_b.caveat: Shows only this study's own single-item measure; one study cannot show what studies mainly use.

10.2307_2580392#E2.says: The authors report that other analyses frequently treat the single fairness item as an interval scale, which indicates single-item measurement in other studies (cited Glass & Fujimoto 1994; Lennon & Rosenfield 1994), but give no count of studies.

10.2307_2580392#E3.says: The whole model (routine and sporadic split, ideology, equity, controls) accounts for an estimated .21 of the latent variance for husbands and .16 for wives, so the actual split alone explains at most that much; the paper does not report the share due to the split alone.
10.2307_2580392#E3.quote:
This measure is an estimate of the proportion of variance that would be
accounted for by the model in unfairness to the wife, if the latter were mea-
sured as a continuous variable. These values are .21 for husbands and .16 for
wives.

tier_b.caveat: Whole-model latent R2 for dichotomised unfair-to-wife outcome; bounds the split's share at .21/.16 but its own share is not reported.

10.2307_2580392#E4.says: Related to the unexplained share, the authors argue that the factors besides actual contribution matter, since a given split is perceived differently depending on other factors.
10.2307_2580392#E4.quote:
For a given division of labor in the home, however,
other factors are also likely to influence perceptions of fairness.

10.2307_2580392#E5.says: Comparison with similarly placed others (social comparison) is described as a theoretical mechanism, attributed to Lennon & Rosenfield; this paper does not measure comparison referents, and its own power measure (wives' human capital) showed little effect.
10.2307_2580392#E5.quote:
Moreover, they tend to make social comparisons with other wives who are
similarly powerless.

tier_b.caveat: Passage is theory attributed to Lennon & Rosenfield; it does not show this paper's own power-measure result.

10.2307_2580392#E6.says: Wives' alternatives, the paper's closest stand-in for the power and comparison account, were measured only through human capital and had little effect on either partner's perceived fairness, so the paper gives no support for referent effects.
10.2307_2580392#E6.quote:
The failure of factors tapping wives' general human capital to have much
effect on perceptions of housework fairness for either partner was not entirely
unexpected.

10.2307_2580392#E7.says: Net of the routine split, husbands' relative contributions to sporadic chores, child care, health and paid hours predicted lower perceived unfairness to the wife; these are objective compensating contributions that stand in for justifications, not justifications the respondent states.
10.2307_2580392#E7.quote:
The
greater the husband's relative contribution to sporadic chores and to child care,
and the better his health relative to his wife's, the less likely either partner was
to say that housework was unfair to the wife.

10.2307_2580392#E8.says: The authors set out the equity account in terms of partners judging a wife's larger share of chores to be justified by the husband's greater inputs elsewhere.
10.2307_2580392#E8.quote:
individuals will feel that women's greater contributions to house-
work are justified.

tier_b.caveat: Introduction states the equity hypothesis; it is an expectation, not a finding that accepted justifications predict fairness.

10.2307_2580392#E9.says: Ideology (endorsement of housework sharing) predicted perceived fairness after the routine split was controlled; the authors read this as the husband's motivation for doing housework shaping whether the arrangement is accepted as fair.
10.2307_2580392#E9.quote:
These patterns suggest that the motivation behind
husbands' housework is a key factor in partners' evaluations of their division of
labor.

tier_b.caveat: Ideology is general sharing/sex-role attitudes, not measured justifications; the motivation reading is the authors' interpretation.

10.2307_2580392#E10.says: For wives only, the husband's sporadic-hours ratio has a significantly stronger effect (p<.002) than the routine-hours ratio; this shows that task type matters net of the other ratio, but both are measured as hours ratios and the test does not separate type from time.
10.2307_2580392#E10.quote:
a test of the equality of coefficients for routine and
sporadic housework reveals that for wives (but not husbands), husbands'
contributions to sporadic housework have a significantly (p <.002) stronger
effect on wives' perceptions of fairness than husbands' contributions to routine
housework.

10.2307_2580392#E11.says: Routine and sporadic chores are entered as separate terms because only time in "female-typed" tasks is held to offset the gender gap; the authors note that equal hours in routine and sporadic tasks are not equivalent, which argues that the type of chore matters beyond hours.
10.2307_2580392#E11.quote:
Therefore men's time in sporadic housework is not
equivalent to women's time in routine housework.

tier_b.caveat: Modelling rationale resting on cited literature and hour distributions; does not test chore type against time as predictors of fairness.

10.2307_2580392#E12.says: Table 3, wives' reports: the share seeing routine housework as unfair to the wife is .371 when the wife does more, against .115 when the husband does more; the corresponding sporadic-task shares are .455 and .287; the gradient differs by chore type, but the table is a bivariate cross-tabulation on ratios of hours.

tier_b.caveat: Bivariate cross-tabulation of hours ratios; does not separate chore type from time spent.

10.2307_2580392#E13.says: The authors do not test whether partners' self-reports sum above 100 percent; they assume exaggeration of hours is randomly distributed across genders and applies equally to both partners' hours, so over-claiming by self is neither measured nor excluded.
10.2307_2580392#E13.quote:
We assume further that the tendency to
report exaggerated hours in housework will be randomly distributed across genders, and
should apply equally to hours reported for either partner.

10.2307_2580392#E14.says: The authors acknowledge that perceived fairness may feed back on reported hours, so the reported split and perceived fairness may be partly the same judgment, which bears on how much variation the "actual" split can explain.
10.2307_2580392#E14.quote:
But perceptions of housework justice may also distort
partners' recall of the time each spouse has actually spent doing housework.
